e.etymology: A modern American coinage, a spelling of Jaylen, which builds on Jay and was made popular by basketball player Jalen Rose. With -lin it also reads as Jay plus Lynn.
A modern spelling that sits between Kaia and Kaya. Kaia is a Scandinavian short form of Katarina and is also linked with Hawaiian kai, sea; Kaiya itself has no single source.
From Trenton, the capital of New Jersey, named Trent's town after the colonial merchant William Trent. As a first name it also serves as a longer form of Trent.

assoc.t: Trenton, capital of New Jersey

e.etymology: A spelling of Jasmine, the fragrant flowering vine, whose name reached English through French and Arabic from Persian yasaman.

assoc.t: Princess Jasmine of Disney's Aladdin (same sound)

e.etymology: The English animal word, first a nickname and now a given name; it has been in the US top 1,000 for boys since 2018. Older bear names include Bjorn and Orson.

assoc.t: The Bear, FX series set in a Chicago restaurant kitchen
bear: gay slang for a big, hairy man

e.etymology: A spelling of Alison, a medieval French pet form of Alice that the Normans brought to England. Alice comes from Old High German Adalhaid, of noble kind.
A spelling of Aidan, from Irish Aodhán, a pet form of Aodh, fire, borne by a 7th-century Irish saint. Aden is also the Yemeni port city on the Gulf of Aden.

assoc.t: Aden, port city in Yemen on the Gulf of Aden

e.etymology: A surname of uncertain origin, used as a first name in the United States since the 1980s. It recalls Gatlinburg, Tennessee, and country music's Gatlin Brothers.

assoc.t: Larry Gatlin and the Gatlin Brothers, country group

e.note: Sounds like Gatling, as in the Gatling gun, an early machine gun.

e.etymology: Spanish and Portuguese for saints, from Latin sanctus. It began as a name for children born around All Saints' Day and is also a very common surname.

assoc.t: Santos, Brazilian port city and Pelé's soccer club

e.etymology: An English place name and surname from Old English stan, stone, and leah, clearing. In America it also served as an English stand-in for the Polish Stanisław.

assoc.t: Stanley Cup, the NHL championship trophy
Stanley, maker of the Quencher tumblers and thermoses
Stanley, hand tool brand
Flat Stanley, children's book character

e.etymology: From the medieval name Lanzo, a short form of Germanic names beginning with land. It has long been tied to the lance, the knight's spear, and used as a short form of Lancelot.
namesakes: Lance Armstrong (cyclist stripped of seven Tour de France titles)

assoc.t: lance, the long spear carried by knights
Lance Armstrong, cyclist stripped of Tour de France titles
Lance, sandwich cracker snack brand

e.etymology: A pet form of Andrea, and sometimes Andrew, from Greek andreios, manly or brave. The -ie spelling is used almost only for girls.
namesakes: Andie MacDowell (actress in Groundhog Day and Four Weddings and a Funeral)

e.etymology: From Hebrew Devorah, bee. Deborah was the prophetess and judge who led Israel to victory in the Book of Judges. It was a top-ten American girls' name from 1950 to 1962.
namesakes: Deborah Kerr (film star of The King and I)

e.etymology: A pet form of Ronald, the Scottish form of Old Norse Rögnvaldr, from words for counsel and ruler. For girls it is a pet form of Veronica.
namesakes: Ronnie Spector (lead singer of the Ronettes)

e.etymology: The feminine of Giovanni, the Italian form of John, from Hebrew Yochanan, God is gracious. It corresponds to Joan and Jane; Gianna is its short form.
A spelling of the Arabic Yusuf, the form of Joseph, from Hebrew Yosef, he will add. Joseph is a prophet in the Qur'an, and the name is used by Arab Christians and Jews as well as Muslims.
A respelling of Madison, an English surname meaning son of Maud, or of Mad, a medieval short form of Matthew. Madison became a girls' name after the 1984 film Splash.

assoc.t: Madison, capital of Wisconsin (same sound)

e.etymology: A 20th-century short form of Briana, the feminine of the Irish Brian, which probably comes from a Celtic word for high or noble.
A modern American coinage in the family of Kayla, Layla and Zara, with the fashionable Z opening. It has no settled meaning.
The spelling of Rebecca used in the King James Old Testament, from Hebrew Rivqah, probably from a root meaning to tie or bind. Rebekah was the wife of Isaac and the mother of Jacob and Esau.
From Arabic Salma, from the root s-l-m, safety and peace, shared with Salim and salaam. Its American rise in the late 1990s followed the actress Salma Hayek.

assoc.t: Salma Hayek, Mexican-American actress

e.etymology: A pet form of Oliver, Olivia and Olive, all tied to Latin oliva, olive. It was given on its own to both boys and girls in the late 1800s.

assoc.t: ollie, the basic skateboarding jump
Ollie's Bargain Outlet, discount store chain

e.etymology: A modern coinage with no settled source. It is often linked with Greek xylon, wood, the root of xylophone, and it matches the sound of Zyla and Kyla.
A pet form of Rick, from Richard, a Germanic name joining ric, ruler, and hard, strong or brave. It also serves as a short form of Ricardo, Enrique and Frederick.
namesakes: Ricky Martin (pop singer of Livin' la Vida Loca)
Ricky Gervais (comedian, creator of The Office)
Ricky Ricardo (Desi Arnaz's character on I Love Lucy)

assoc.t: Ricky Ricardo, Lucy's husband on I Love Lucy

e.etymology: From Hebrew Yedidyah, beloved of Yahweh. In the Bible it is the blessing name the prophet Nathan gave to the infant Solomon.
A modern spelling of Harmony, the English word for musical agreement and peaceful accord, from Greek harmonia. Harmonia was the Greek goddess of concord.
A pet form of Edward, Edwin, Edgar and Edmund, all built on Old English ead, wealth or fortune. It has been given as a name in its own right since the 1800s.

assoc.t: Eddie, the skeletal mascot of the band Iron Maiden
Eddie Bauer, outdoor clothing brand

e.etymology: A spelling of Kian favored by Indian families. Kian is a Persian name meaning kings or royal, after the legendary Kayanian dynasty; the Irish Cian, ancient, sounds the same.
From Tallulah Falls and the Tallulah River in Georgia, a Native American place name of uncertain meaning. Actress Tallulah Bankhead, named for her grandmother, made it known.

assoc.t: Tallulah Gorge, state park and waterfalls in north Georgia
Tallulah Bankhead, husky-voiced stage and film star

e.etymology: A form of the biblical Jair, from Hebrew Ya'ir, he will give light. It surged among Mexican American families in 2002 and 2003 with the Mexican pop singer Yahir.
A respelling of Waylon, a form of Wayland, the legendary smith of Germanic myth. Waylon became an American name through country singer Waylon Jennings.

assoc.t: Waylon Jennings, outlaw country singer (same sound)

e.etymology: An English surname from villages named Dutton: in Cheshire from Old English dun, hill, and tun, settlement; in Lancashire from Dudda's settlement. Its rise follows the Dutton family of TV's Yellowstone.

assoc.t: the Duttons, ranching family of the TV drama Yellowstone
Dutton, book publishing imprint
